doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

title: Finishing the Jazz Singers book and writing style
summary: He had to cut off the book at 500 singers, avoids repeating adjectives and writes spontaneously with little outline.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Um hum. Well a book like your Jazz Singers takes some serious organization and planning. How do you know when you’re done with a book like this?

The thing is it’s kind of crazy because there are so many singers, and you know when I was writing the book it seemed like I’d discover five new singers, five current singers that were new every week. So it was getting to the point where if I don’t cut off the book now it’s going to be three times as big. When I did a book on jazz guitarists then there would be maybe one new guitarist a week. But with singers it just seemed like they were all over the place. And most of them are good. So it was difficult because I wanted to include a lot of local singers who were talented and who grew up to become famous. So that’s why my list had 500 and it could have been 2000 really. But I had to cut it off finally. There are other ones, but in the current scene there were just so many.
It would have been an extremely thick book also.

I was wondering about your choice of adjectives, using words to describe the singers right off the bat, do you have, I’m almost picturing a list of adjectives that you go to that you think are relevant for this person and that you haven’t used in a while.

Yeah pretty much. You know the hardest part about writing a book like that where you’re describing the style of maybe 500 people is not to have too much repetition. So if you call someone colorful you don’t want to use that word too soon again. Maybe four entries later. It’s just a matter of making them readable really. A lot of them are similar to each other anyway. So no, I didn’t have a list really, just whatever comes. And that’s usually how I write. I usually don’t write with an outline either. outline just so I know how a book’s going to progress but in general it’s pretty spontaneous. And then I’ll go back and proofread it several times and fix anything that might have been repetitious or didn’t fit.
